about: Dynamics and Relativity is a 24-lecture Lent Term course in Part IA of the Cambridge Mathematical Tripos, and assumes familiarity with the non-examinable Mechanics course. Following the official schedule it covers frames and Newton's laws, the dynamics of a single particle (energy, oscillations, orbits, Rutherford scattering, rotating frames), systems of particles and rockets, rigid bodies, and special relativity up to 4-momentum and particle collisions. It is examined on Paper 4 alongside Numbers and Sets; each Part IA paper has a Section I of shorter questions and a Section II of longer ones, and the course is not examined for students taking Option (b), Mathematics with Physics. The Foucault pendulum is starred, so not examinable.
topics: Basic concepts: frames, Newton's laws, dimensions and forces
Particle dynamics: polar coordinates, work and potential energy
Angular momentum, orbits and Rutherford scattering
Rotating frames: centrifugal and Coriolis forces
Systems of particles, the two-body problem and rockets
Rigid bodies: moments of inertia and rolling

notes.h: Basic concepts: frames, Newton's laws, dimensions and forces
notes.body:
The course begins by setting out the framework of Newtonian mechanics carefully, because the final part of the course (special relativity, seven of the 24 lectures) replaces part of it. Familiarity with the non-examinable Mechanics course is assumed.

Frames and Galilean transformations
- A frame of reference is a choice of origin, axes and clock. An inertial frame is one in which a free particle moves with constant velocity (Newton's first law).
- If S′ moves with constant velocity v relative to S, with axes parallel and origins coinciding at t = 0, the Galilean transformation is r′ = r − vt, t′ = t.
- Velocities then add (u′ = u − v), and accelerations are the same in both frames. So if F = ma holds in S it holds in S′: the laws of Newtonian mechanics take the same form in every inertial frame (Galilean relativity).
- Time is absolute in Galilean physics: t′ = t. Special relativity drops this.

Newton's laws
- First: a body not acted on by a force moves at constant velocity. This really defines inertial frames.
- Second: F = dp/dt with p = mv; for constant mass F = ma.
- Third: forces between two particles are equal and opposite. In the strong form they also act along the line joining the particles, which is needed for angular momentum conservation later.

Dimensional analysis
- Every physical quantity has dimensions built from mass M, length L and time T. Force has dimensions MLT⁻², energy ML²T⁻², and Newton's constant G has M⁻¹L³T⁻².
- Equations must be dimensionally consistent, which lets you guess the form of an answer up to a dimensionless constant.
- Example: the period of a simple pendulum can depend only on m, l and g. The only combination with dimensions of time is √(l/g) (m cannot appear), so T = C√(l/g). Solving the equation gives C = 2π for small swings.
- Example: the period of a circular orbit of radius a about a mass M depends on a and GM (dimensions L³T⁻²). So T ∝ a^(3/2)/√(GM), which is Kepler's third law up to a constant.

Examples of forces
- Gravity: F = −(GMm/r²) r̂ on m due to M at the origin; near the Earth's surface this is approximately the constant force mg.
- Friction: static friction can take any value up to μₛN; once sliding, kinetic friction has magnitude μₖN and opposes the relative motion.
- Drag: roughly linear in speed at low speeds and quadratic at higher speeds.
- Lorentz force on a charge q: F = q(E + v × B). The magnetic part is perpendicular to v, so it does no work. In a uniform field B with v ⊥ B the particle moves in a circle of radius mv/(qB) with angular frequency qB/m (the cyclotron frequency), independent of speed.

Exam tips: in a dimensional analysis question, write the dimensions of each quantity first and solve for the exponents explicitly; say which quantities you assume the answer depends on.

notes.h: Particle dynamics: polar coordinates, work and potential energy
notes.body:
The eight lectures on a single particle start with the equation of motion in different coordinates and the idea of energy.

Plane polar coordinates
- With e_r = (cos θ, sin θ) and e_θ = (−sin θ, cos θ): de_r/dt = θ̇ e_θ and de_θ/dt = −θ̇ e_r.
- Position r = r e_r. Velocity: v = ṙ e_r + rθ̇ e_θ.
- Acceleration: a = (r̈ − rθ̇²) e_r + (rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇) e_θ, and the transverse part equals (1/r) d(r²θ̇)/dt.
- The −rθ̇² term is the centripetal acceleration. These are genuine acceleration terms in an inertial frame, not the fictitious forces of rotating frames.
- Example: circular motion r = a has a = −aθ̇² e_r + aθ̈ e_θ.

Work and kinetic energy
- The kinetic energy is T = ½m|v|². From m dv/dt = F, dT/dt = F·v (the power).
- Integrating: the change in T equals the work done, W = ∫ F·dr along the path.

Conservative forces and potential energy
- F is conservative if the work done between two points is independent of the path; equivalently F = −∇V for a potential energy V, and (on a simply connected region) ∇ × F = 0.
- Then the total energy E = ½m|v|² + V(r) is constant. Proof: dE/dt = mv·v̇ + ∇V·v = v·(F + ∇V) = 0.
- Gravity: V = −GMm/r. Near the surface, V = mgz. A linear spring: V = ½kx².
- Friction and drag are not conservative: they always remove mechanical energy.

One-dimensional motion in a potential
- E = ½mẋ² + V(x) gives ẋ = ±√(2(E − V(x))/m). Motion is only possible where V(x) ≤ E; points with V(x) = E are turning points.
- Sketching V(x) and a horizontal line at height E shows at once whether motion is bounded (trapped between two turning points) or unbounded.
- The time between positions is t = ∫ dx/√(2(E − V)/m).

Escape velocity
- A particle leaving the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R escapes (reaches infinity) if E = ½mv² − GMm/R ≥ 0, so v ≥ √(2GM/R). For the Earth this is about 11.2 km/s.
- Notice the escape speed does not depend on direction (ignoring the atmosphere and rotation), since energy is a scalar.

Exam tips: when a question says "show energy is conserved", differentiate E with respect to time and use the equation of motion; in polar coordinates, derive the acceleration rather than quoting it if the question asks for it.

Most of physics is about small oscillations about an equilibrium. This part of the course shows how the shape of the potential determines stability and frequency, and what damping does.

Equilibria and stability (one dimension)
- With F = −V′(x), equilibrium points x₀ satisfy V′(x₀) = 0.
- If V″(x₀) > 0 (a minimum of V) the equilibrium is stable; if V″(x₀) < 0 (a maximum) it is unstable. If V″(x₀) = 0, look at higher derivatives.
- Small oscillations: put x = x₀ + ξ and Taylor expand. mξ̈ = −V′(x₀ + ξ) ≈ −V″(x₀)ξ. So near a stable equilibrium the motion is simple harmonic with ω = √(V″(x₀)/m), period 2π/ω.
- Example: V(x) = k(x⁴/4 − x²/2) with k > 0. V′ = k(x³ − x), so equilibria at x = 0 and x = ±1. V″ = k(3x² − 1): at x = 0 it is −k (unstable); at x = ±1 it is 2k (stable), with ω = √(2k/m).
- Simple pendulum (length l): V = −mgl cos θ, the equation is θ̈ = −(g/l) sin θ, and small oscillations have ω = √(g/l). The upside-down position θ = π is unstable.

Damping
- A linear damping force −cẋ added to a spring force −kx gives mẍ + cẋ + kx = 0. Write it as ẍ + 2γẋ + ω₀²x = 0 with 2γ = c/m and ω₀² = k/m.
- Trying x = e^(λt): λ = −γ ± √(γ² − ω₀²).
- Underdamped (γ < ω₀): x = Ae^(−γt) cos(ωt − φ), with ω = √(ω₀² − γ²). Decaying oscillations at a lower frequency than ω₀.
- Critically damped (γ = ω₀): x = (A + Bt)e^(−γt). Returns to equilibrium fastest without oscillating.
- Overdamped (γ > ω₀): x = Ae^(λ₁t) + Be^(λ₂t), both λ negative and real. Slow non-oscillatory return.
- Energy: E = ½mẋ² + ½kx² satisfies dE/dt = −cẋ² ≤ 0, so damping always removes energy.

Stability with damping
- A stable equilibrium of the undamped system remains stable with damping, but is now asymptotically stable: the particle settles at x₀ instead of oscillating for ever.

Reading a potential graph
- Draw V(x) and a line at the energy E. Minima of V are stable equilibria; between turning points the particle oscillates; near a maximum of V it can sit in unstable equilibrium or pass slowly over the top.
- An orbit with E exactly equal to a local maximum of V takes infinite time to reach that point.

Exam tips: always check the sign of V″ at each equilibrium and give the frequency as √(V″/m); in damping questions identify the regime by comparing γ with ω₀ before writing a solution.

notes.h: Angular momentum, orbits and Rutherford scattering
notes.body:
Orbits are a central part of the single-particle dynamics; long questions often involve deriving and using the u(θ) equation.

Angular momentum and central forces
- Angular momentum about O: L = r × p; torque G = r × F; dL/dt = G.
- A central force F = f(r) r̂ has zero torque about O, so L is constant. Then the motion lies in a fixed plane, and in plane polars r²θ̇ = h is constant (h = |L|/m).
- Kepler's second law follows: the area swept out satisfies dA/dt = ½r²θ̇ = h/2, constant.

Energy and the effective potential
- E = ½m(ṙ² + r²θ̇²) + V(r) = ½mṙ² + mh²/(2r²) + V(r).
- So the radial motion is one-dimensional in the effective potential V_eff(r) = V(r) + mh²/(2r²). The extra term is the "centrifugal barrier".
- Circular orbits sit at stationary points of V_eff. Stability: for an attractive power law force of magnitude k/rⁿ, V_eff″ at the circular radius has the sign of 3 − n, so circular orbits are stable if and only if n < 3. The inverse square law (n = 2) is stable.

The u(θ) equation
- Put u = 1/r. Using θ̇ = hu²: ṙ = −h du/dθ and r̈ = −h²u² d²u/dθ².
- The radial equation m(r̈ − rθ̇²) = f gives d²u/dθ² + u = −f/(mh²u²), where f is the radial force component (positive if repulsive).

Gravity and Kepler's laws
- With f = −GMm/r² = −GMmu²: d²u/dθ² + u = GM/h². So u = (GM/h²)(1 + e cos(θ − θ₀)), i.e. r = ℓ/(1 + e cos(θ − θ₀)) with ℓ = h²/(GM).
- This is a conic with a focus at O: ellipse (e < 1), parabola (e = 1), hyperbola (e > 1). Equivalently E < 0, E = 0, E > 0. For an ellipse of semi-major axis a, ℓ = a(1 − e²) and E = −GMm/(2a).
- Kepler I: planets move on ellipses with the Sun at a focus. Kepler II: equal areas in equal times. Kepler III: T² = 4π²a³/(GM), from T = (area πab)/(h/2) with b = a√(1 − e²) and h² = GMa(1 − e²).
- Circular orbit speed √(GM/r); escape speed √(2GM/r).

Rutherford scattering
- A repulsive inverse square force, f = k/r² with k > 0 (e.g. Coulomb repulsion between like charges), gives d²u/dθ² + u = −k/(mh²). Orbits are hyperbolae that bend away from the centre of force, which sits at the focus on the outside (convex side) of the branch.
- If the particle comes in from infinity with speed v and impact parameter b (so h = bv), the deflection angle χ satisfies tan(χ/2) = k/(mv²b).
- Sketch: with the particle arriving from θ = π, the solution is u = −(k/(mh²))(1 + cos θ) + (1/b) sin θ; it leaves along the other root of u = 0, θ = χ, where tan(χ/2) = bk/(mh²).
- Small impact parameter means large deflection; head-on (b → 0) gives χ → π.

Exam tips: state clearly that L is conserved because the force is central; derive ṙ = −h du/dθ explicitly; and match constants using conditions at a particular point (perihelion or infinity).

notes.h: Rotating frames: centrifugal and Coriolis forces
notes.body:
The Earth rotates, and many practical problems are easiest in a rotating frame. The price is fictitious forces.

Rates of change in rotating frames
- Let frame S′ rotate with angular velocity ω relative to an inertial frame S, with a common origin. For any vector A: (dA/dt)_S = (dA/dt)_S′ + ω × A.
- Applying this twice to the position r: a_S = a_S′ + 2ω × v_S′ + ω × (ω × r) + ω̇ × r.

Equation of motion in a rotating frame
- m a_S′ = F − 2mω × v_S′ − mω × (ω × r) − mω̇ × r.
- −2mω × v is the Coriolis force; −mω × (ω × r) is the centrifugal force; −mω̇ × r (the Euler force) vanishes for constant ω.
- These are not real forces: they arise only because S′ is not inertial.

Centrifugal force
- −mω × (ω × r) = mω²r⊥, where r⊥ is the component of r perpendicular to the axis. It points directly away from the axis with magnitude mω²d (d is the distance from the axis).
- It is conservative, with potential −½m|ω × r|².
- On Earth it combines with gravity to give the effective gravity g_eff = g − ω × (ω × r). At the equator g is reduced by ω²R ≈ 0.034 m/s², and a plumb line does not point exactly at the Earth's centre except at the poles and the equator.

Coriolis force
- −2mω × v is perpendicular to v, so it does no work and only changes the direction of motion.
- In the northern hemisphere it deflects horizontal motion to the right; in the southern hemisphere to the left. This is why large weather systems circulate anticlockwise around low pressure in the northern hemisphere.
- Falling bodies are deflected eastwards. For a body dropped from height h at latitude λ, the leading-order deflection is (1/3)ωg t³ cos λ with t = √(2h/g). At the equator from h = 100 m this is about 2.2 cm.
- The Earth's angular velocity is ω = 2π per sidereal day ≈ 7.29 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s.

Worked example: bead on a rotating wire
- A bead slides on a smooth straight wire rotating in a horizontal plane at constant ω about a vertical axis through one end. In the rotating frame the bead's distance r from the axis obeys r̈ = ω²r (centrifugal), so r = Ae^(ωt) + Be^(−ωt).
- The Coriolis force is balanced by the wire's normal reaction, of magnitude 2mωṙ. (Check in the inertial frame: the transverse equation gives N = m(1/r) d(r²ω)/dt = 2mωṙ.)

Non-examinable
- The Foucault pendulum is starred in the schedule, so it cannot be examined; it illustrates the Coriolis force making a pendulum's plane of swing precess.

Exam tips: write the full equation with all fictitious terms before simplifying, state which terms vanish (e.g. ω constant), and check directions with a careful right-hand-rule sketch.

notes.h: Systems of particles, the two-body problem and rockets
notes.body:
Two lectures extend the single-particle results to many particles, including the two-body problem and variable mass.

Momentum and the centre of mass
- For particles mᵢ at rᵢ, the total mass is M = Σmᵢ and the centre of mass is R = (1/M)Σmᵢrᵢ.
- Total momentum P = Σmᵢṙᵢ = MṘ.
- Internal forces cancel in pairs (Newton's third law), so dP/dt = F_ext: the centre of mass moves like a single particle of mass M acted on by the total external force. With no external force, P is conserved.

Angular momentum
- L = Σ rᵢ × mᵢṙᵢ. If internal forces are central (act along the lines joining particles), their torques cancel and dL/dt = Σ rᵢ × Fᵢ^ext.
- Decomposition: writing rᵢ = R + sᵢ with Σmᵢsᵢ = 0, L = R × P + Σ sᵢ × mᵢṡᵢ: angular momentum of the centre of mass plus angular momentum about the centre of mass.

Energy
- Kinetic energy splits similarly: T = ½M|Ṙ|² + Σ ½mᵢ|ṡᵢ|².
- If all forces (internal and external) are conservative, total energy T + V is conserved.

The two-body problem
- Two particles interact by a force F(r) on particle 1 due to 2, where r = r₁ − r₂, with no external forces.
- The centre of mass moves uniformly. The separation obeys μr̈ = F(r), with reduced mass μ = m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂).
- So the two-body problem reduces to a one-body problem in which a particle of mass μ moves in the fixed force field F.
- For gravity, F = −Gm₁m₂ r/r³, which gives r̈ = −G(m₁ + m₂) r/r³, so Kepler's third law becomes T² = 4π²a³/(G(m₁ + m₂)).

Variable mass: the rocket equation
- A rocket of mass m(t) and velocity v ejects fuel at speed u relative to itself, backwards. In time δt it loses mass −δm (δm < 0).
- Momentum balance: (m + δm)(v + δv) + (−δm)(v − u) − mv = F δt. To first order, m δv + u δm = F δt.
- So m dv/dt = −u dm/dt + F. The term −u dm/dt is positive (dm/dt < 0): this is the thrust.
- With F = 0: v − v₀ = u ln(m₀/m), Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation. To gain speed 3u the mass ratio m₀/m must be e³ ≈ 20.
- Vertical launch in uniform gravity with constant burn rate α (m = m₀ − αt): dv/dt = uα/(m₀ − αt) − g, so v = u ln(m₀/(m₀ − αt)) − gt while the fuel lasts. The rocket only lifts off if uα > m₀g.

Common slip
- Do not apply F = d(mv)/dt naively to a rocket: the ejected fuel carries momentum away, and only the momentum balance of the whole system is correct.

Exam tips: in rocket questions, write the momentum at time t and at t + δt for the whole system (rocket plus ejected fuel) and take the limit; state the frame in which you measure each velocity.

notes.h: Rigid bodies: moments of inertia and rolling
notes.body:
Three lectures treat rigid bodies, concentrating on rotation about a fixed axis and simple combined rotation and translation.

Rotation about a fixed axis
- A rigid body rotating with angular velocity ω about a fixed axis: each point moves with velocity ω × r.
- Moment of inertia about the axis: I = Σmᵢdᵢ² (or ∫ d² dm), where dᵢ is the distance from the axis.
- Kinetic energy T = ½Iω², angular momentum component along the axis L = Iω, and the equation of motion is Iω̇ = G (torque about the axis).

Standard moments of inertia (mass M)
- Thin rod, length L: ML²/12 about a perpendicular axis through its centre; ML²/3 about an end.
- Ring or hoop of radius a, about its axis: Ma². Uniform disc or solid cylinder about its axis: Ma²/2.
- Solid sphere about a diameter: (2/5)Ma². Thin spherical shell: (2/3)Ma².
- Example calculation for a disc: I = ∫₀^a r² (M/(πa²)) 2πr dr = Ma²/2.

Parallel axis theorem
- I = I_cm + Md², where I_cm is about a parallel axis through the centre of mass and d is the distance between the axes.
- Proof: write each position as R + sᵢ relative to the centre of mass; the cross term 2Σmᵢ(R⊥·sᵢ⊥) vanishes because Σmᵢsᵢ = 0.
- Example: rod about its end, ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/3.

Combined rotation and translation
- For a body moving in a plane, T = ½MV² + ½I_cm ω², where V is the speed of the centre of mass.
- The centre of mass obeys MV̇ = F_ext, and rotation about the centre of mass obeys I_cm ω̇ = torque about the centre of mass.

Rolling without slipping
- The contact point is instantaneously at rest: V = aω for a wheel or ball of radius a.
- Friction at the contact does no work in pure rolling, so energy is conserved.
- Down a slope of angle α from rest through height h: Mgh = ½MV² + ½I V²/a², so V² = 2gh/(1 + I/(Ma²)), and the acceleration is g sin α/(1 + I/(Ma²)).
- Sphere: (5/7)g sin α. Solid cylinder: (2/3)g sin α. Hoop: (1/2)g sin α. A larger I/(Ma²) means a slower roll.
- Friction needed for a sphere: F = (2/7)Mg sin α, so it rolls without slipping only if μ ≥ (2/7) tan α.

Compound pendulum
- A body pivoted at distance d from its centre of mass: Iθ̈ = −Mgd sin θ, with I about the pivot. Small oscillations have ω² = Mgd/I.
- Uniform rod pivoted at one end: I = ML²/3, d = L/2, so ω² = 3g/(2L).

From sliding to rolling
- A uniform ball is set sliding with speed v₀ and no spin on a rough horizontal table. Friction slows it and spins it up until V = aω. Angular momentum about the contact point is conserved (friction and the normal reaction act there, and the weight and normal reaction cancel), so Mv₀a = MVa + (2/5)Ma²(V/a), giving V = 5v₀/7.

Exam tips: always say which point you take moments about; for rolling problems use energy for speeds and Newton's laws plus torques for forces.

The last seven lectures replace Galilean relativity with Einstein's special relativity. The first half concerns how coordinates change between frames.

The postulates
- The principle of relativity: the laws of physics take the same form in all inertial frames.
- The speed of light in vacuum, c, is the same in all inertial frames.
- Together these force us to abandon absolute time: different inertial observers disagree about which events are simultaneous.

Lorentz transformation (1 + 1 dimensions)
- S′ moves with speed v along the x-axis of S, origins coinciding at t = t′ = 0. With β = v/c and γ = 1/√(1 − β²):
- ct′ = γ(ct − βx), x′ = γ(x − βct), and y′ = y, z′ = z in 3 + 1 dimensions.
- The inverse has v replaced by −v. As v/c → 0, γ → 1 and we recover the Galilean transformation.
- Rapidity: write β = tanh φ, so γ = cosh φ and γβ = sinh φ. Then ct′ = ct cosh φ − x sinh φ, x′ = −ct sinh φ + x cosh φ: a "hyperbolic rotation". Successive boosts along the same axis add rapidities.

The invariant interval
- For two events separated by (cΔt, Δx, Δy, Δz), the interval Δs² = c²Δt² − Δx² − Δy² − Δz² is the same in all inertial frames. (This is the sign convention, with Minkowski metric diag(1, −1, −1, −1); some books use the opposite overall sign.)
- Timelike separation (Δs² > 0): one event can influence the other, and all observers agree on their time order. Spacelike (Δs² < 0): no causal connection, and the order can differ between frames. Null (Δs² = 0): connected by a light signal.

Consequences
- Relativity of simultaneity: events with Δt = 0 and Δx ≠ 0 in S have Δt′ = −γvΔx/c² in S′.
- Time dilation: a clock at rest in S′ (Δx′ = 0) ticks Δt′; in S the interval is Δt = γΔt′. Moving clocks run slow.
- Length contraction: a rod at rest in S′ with length L₀, measured in S by marking both ends at the same time t, has length L = L₀/γ. Lengths perpendicular to the motion are unchanged.
- Example: muons with mean life 2.2 μs (in their rest frame) moving at 0.995c have γ ≈ 10, so in the lab they travel on average about 6.6 km, not 660 m.

Velocity addition
- A particle with velocity u′ along x in S′ has velocity u = (u′ + v)/(1 + u′v/c²) in S.
- Example: 0.6c ⊕ 0.6c = 1.2c/1.36 = (15/17)c ≈ 0.88c. If u′ = c then u = c: light has speed c in every frame.

Spacetime diagrams
- Plot ct against x. Light rays are at 45°. The ct′ axis (x′ = 0) is the line x = βct, and the x′ axis (t′ = 0) is ct = βx: both tilt towards the light line as β grows.

Exam tips: in paradox questions, identify the events, write their coordinates in one frame and transform; never mix time dilation and length contraction formulae without saying which observer measures what.

The course ends with the 4-vector formalism, which makes relativistic dynamics, particle decays and collisions mechanical to compute.

4-vectors
- The position 4-vector is X = (ct, x). Any 4-component object that transforms like X under Lorentz transformations is a 4-vector.
- The Minkowski inner product X·Y = X⁰Y⁰ − X¹Y¹ − X²Y² − X³Y³ is Lorentz invariant. In particular X·X is the invariant interval.

Proper time and 4-velocity
- Along a particle's world line, proper time τ is time measured by a clock carried by the particle: dτ = dt/γ(u), where u is the particle's speed.
- 4-velocity U = dX/dτ = γ(u)(c, u). It satisfies U·U = γ²(c² − u²) = c².

4-momentum
- For a particle of (rest) mass m: P = mU = (E/c, p), with E = γmc² and p = γmu.
- P·P = m²c² gives E² = |p|²c² + m²c⁴. A particle at rest has E = mc².
- Newtonian limit: γ ≈ 1 + u²/(2c²), so E ≈ mc² + ½mu² and p ≈ mu: the rest energy plus Newtonian kinetic energy.
- Massless particles such as photons have P·P = 0, so E = |p|c and they travel at c. For a photon E = hf.

Conservation of 4-momentum
- In any decay or collision of isolated particles, the total 4-momentum is conserved: energy and momentum together.
- Rest mass is not separately conserved. Kinetic energy can be converted into rest mass and vice versa.
- Example: two particles of mass m collide head-on with speeds u and stick. Momentum is zero, energy 2γ(u)mc², so the product has mass 2γ(u)m, more than 2m.

Decay of a particle at rest
- A particle of mass M at rest decays into particles of masses m₁ and m₂. Momentum conservation gives equal and opposite momenta p. Write P = P₁ + P₂ and square P₂ = P − P₁: m₂²c² = M²c² + m₁²c² − 2P·P₁. In the rest frame P = (Mc, 0), so P·P₁ = Mc × E₁/c = ME₁. Hence E₁ = (M² + m₁² − m₂²)c²/(2M).
- Example: a charged pion (about 139.6 MeV/c²) at rest decays to a muon (about 105.7 MeV/c²) and a neutrino (treated as massless). Then E_μ = (m_π² + m_μ²)c²/(2m_π) ≈ 109.8 MeV, so the muon's kinetic energy is about 4.1 MeV.

Collisions and thresholds
- The quantity (P₁ + P₂)·(P₁ + P₂) is invariant. In the centre of momentum frame it equals (E_total/c)², which must be at least (Σ final masses × c)² for the reaction to happen.
- Example: p + p → p + p + p + p̄ with one proton at rest (fixed target). With P₁ = (E/c, p) and P₂ = (mc, 0), (P₁ + P₂)·(P₁ + P₂) = 2m²c² + 2mE, and this must be at least (4mc)². So E ≥ 7mc²: the beam needs kinetic energy at least 6mc².

Exam tips: work with 4-vectors and square them to eliminate unknowns, choose the frame (lab or centre of momentum) where each quantity is easiest, and quote E² = p²c² + m²c⁴ explicitly.

cards.b: r′ = r − vt, t′ = t for S′ moving with constant velocity v relative to S. Accelerations are unchanged, so F = ma holds in both.
A frame in which a free particle (no forces) moves with constant velocity; Newton's laws hold in it.

questions.q: A charged particle moves in a uniform magnetic field with velocity perpendicular to the field. Which statement is true?
options: It moves in a straight line at constant speed
Its angular frequency of rotation is proportional to its speed
questions.why: The magnetic force qv × B is always perpendicular to v, so it does no work and the speed is constant (the particle circles). Kinetic energy therefore cannot increase; the force is non-zero so the path is not straight; and the angular frequency qB/m does not depend on speed (the radius does).

questions.q: By dimensional analysis, the period T of a circular orbit of radius a around a mass M must be proportional to which expression?
questions.why: GM has dimensions L³T⁻², so a^(3/2)/(GM)^(1/2) has dimensions L^(3/2)/(L^(3/2)T⁻¹) = T. √(a/(GM)) has dimensions T/L; a²/(GM) has T²/L; and √(GM/a³) has dimensions T⁻¹, a frequency, not a period.

questions.q: Show that Newton's second law takes the same form in two inertial frames related by a Galilean transformation, and explain why this fails if S′ accelerates relative to S.
markScheme: Writes r′ = r − vt, t′ = t with v constant
Differentiates twice: r̈′ = r̈
Notes forces and masses are frame independent in Newtonian mechanics, so F = mr̈′
If S′ has acceleration A, r̈′ = r̈ − A, so an extra −mA appears (a fictitious force)
questions.modelAnswer: With r′ = r − vt and t′ = t, differentiating with respect to t (= t′) gives ṙ′ = ṙ − v and, since v is constant, r̈′ = r̈. Forces (which depend on relative positions and velocities) and masses are the same in both frames in Newtonian mechanics, so F = mr̈ implies F = mr̈′: the law has the same form. If S′ accelerates, r′ = r − d(t) with d̈ = A ≠ 0, so r̈′ = r̈ − A and mr̈′ = F − mA. The extra term −mA is a fictitious force, so S′ is not inertial.

questions.q: A particle moves on the circle r = a with θ̇ = ω constant. What is its acceleration in plane polars?
questions.why: With r = a, ṙ = r̈ = 0 and θ̈ = 0, so a = (r̈ − rθ̇²)e_r + (rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇)e_θ = −aω² e_r, pointing to the centre. The outward version has the wrong sign; 2aω e_θ wrongly uses the 2ṙθ̇ term, which is zero here; and zero acceleration ignores the change in direction of the velocity.

questions.q: A particle moves in one dimension in the potential V(x) = x² with energy E = 4 (in consistent units). Where can it be found?
questions.why: Kinetic energy E − V must be non-negative, so x² ≤ 4, giving −2 ≤ x ≤ 2 with turning points at ±2. The motion is bounded, so not the whole line; the region x² ≥ 4 is exactly where motion is forbidden; and 0 ≤ x ≤ 4 confuses E with the turning point position.

questions.q: A particle of mass m moves under a force F = −∇V. Show that E = ½m|ṙ|² + V(r) is constant. Hence find the minimum speed with which a projectile must leave the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R to escape to infinity (ignore air resistance and rotation).
markScheme: Differentiates: dE/dt = mṙ·r̈ + ∇V·ṙ
Uses mr̈ = −∇V to get dE/dt = 0
Gravitational potential energy V = −GMm/r
Escape condition: E ≥ 0 (speed ≥ 0 as r → ∞)
v_esc = √(2GM/R)
questions.modelAnswer: dE/dt = mṙ·r̈ + ∇V·ṙ (chain rule, d V(r(t))/dt = ∇V·ṙ). Using mr̈ = −∇V, dE/dt = ṙ·(−∇V + ∇V) = 0, so E is constant. For gravity V = −GMm/r. A projectile leaving r = R with speed v has E = ½mv² − GMm/R. To reach infinity we need ½m|ṙ|² = E + GMm/r ≥ 0 for all r, which as r → ∞ requires E ≥ 0. So ½mv² ≥ GMm/R, i.e. v ≥ √(2GM/R).

questions.q: A particle of mass m moves in V(x) = k(x⁴/4 − x²/2), k > 0. What is the angular frequency of small oscillations about x = 1?
options: There are none, because x = 1 is unstable
questions.why: V″(x) = k(3x² − 1), which is 2k at x = 1, so ω = √(V″/m) = √(2k/m). √(k/m) uses the size of V″ at x = 0 (where V″ = −k) instead of evaluating V″ at x = 1; √(3k/m) forgets the −1 in V″; and x = 1 is a minimum of V (V″ > 0), so it is stable, the unstable point being x = 0.

questions.q: For ẍ + 2γẋ + ω₀²x = 0 with γ = ω₀, which describes the motion?
options: A sum of two different decaying exponentials
x = (A + Bt)e^(−γt), returning to equilibrium without oscillating
questions.why: γ = ω₀ is critical damping, where the characteristic equation has a repeated root −γ, giving (A + Bt)e^(−γt). Decaying oscillations need γ < ω₀ (and here √(ω₀² − γ²) would be 0); undamped oscillations need γ = 0; and two distinct exponentials occur for overdamping, γ > ω₀.

questions.q: A simple pendulum of length l has θ̈ = −(g/l) sin θ. Find its equilibria, determine their stability, and find the period of small oscillations about the stable one.
markScheme: Potential energy V = −mgl cos θ (or direct use of equation)
Equilibria θ = 0 and θ = π
θ = 0 stable (V″ = mgl > 0 or linearised equation θ̈ = −(g/l)θ)
θ = π unstable: with θ = π + ξ, ξ̈ = +(g/l)ξ, exponential growth
Period 2π√(l/g)
questions.modelAnswer: Equilibria need sin θ = 0, so θ = 0 (hanging down) or θ = π (inverted). The potential energy is V = −mgl cos θ, with V″ = mgl cos θ. At θ = 0, V″ = mgl > 0: stable. Linearising, sin θ ≈ θ, so θ̈ = −(g/l)θ, simple harmonic with ω = √(g/l) and period 2π√(l/g). At θ = π, put θ = π + ξ: sin(π + ξ) = −sin ξ ≈ −ξ, so ξ̈ = (g/l)ξ, whose solutions grow like e^(√(g/l) t): unstable (V″ = −mgl < 0).

questions.q: For an attractive central force of magnitude k/rⁿ, for which n are circular orbits stable?
questions.why: At a circular orbit radius the second derivative of the effective potential is proportional to (3 − n), so stability needs n < 3, which includes gravity (n = 2) and the spring force (n = −1). n > 3 gives instability, so does not work; n = 2 is not the only stable case; and n = 4 shows not all positive n work.

questions.q: A comet's orbit around the Sun has positive total energy. What is its shape?
options: A parabola with the Sun at the focus
An ellipse with the Sun at the centre
A hyperbola with the Sun at a focus
An ellipse with the Sun at a focus
questions.why: E > 0 corresponds to e > 1 in r = ℓ/(1 + e cos θ), a hyperbola (an unbound orbit). Ellipses have E < 0 and parabolas E = 0 exactly. In inverse square orbits the attracting body is at a focus, never at the centre of the ellipse.

questions.q: A particle of mass m moves under a central force f(r) r̂. Show that h = r²θ̇ is constant, and derive the orbit equation d²u/dθ² + u = −f/(mh²u²), where u = 1/r.
markScheme: Torque r × f r̂ = 0, so L conserved; or transverse equation (1/r) d(r²θ̇)/dt = 0
θ̇ = hu²
ṙ = −h du/dθ (via dr/dt = (dr/dθ)θ̇)
r̈ = −h²u² d²u/dθ²
Substitutes in m(r̈ − rθ̇²) = f to get the result
questions.modelAnswer: The transverse equation of motion is m(1/r) d(r²θ̇)/dt = 0, since the force is radial, so h = r²θ̇ is constant. (Equivalently, the torque r × f r̂ is zero, so L = mr²θ̇ ẑ is conserved.) With u = 1/r, θ̇ = h/r² = hu². Then ṙ = d(1/u)/dt = −(1/u²)(du/dθ)θ̇ = −h du/dθ, and r̈ = −h (d²u/dθ²) θ̇ = −h²u² d²u/dθ². The radial equation m(r̈ − rθ̇²) = f becomes m(−h²u² u″ − (1/u)h²u⁴) = f, i.e. −mh²u²(u″ + u) = f, so d²u/dθ² + u = −f/(mh²u²).

questions.q: In a frame rotating with constant angular velocity ω, which fictitious force can change a particle's speed?
options: The Euler force, which is non-zero here
Neither: fictitious forces never do work
questions.why: The centrifugal force mω²r⊥ has a component along the velocity whenever the particle moves towards or away from the axis, so it can do work. The Coriolis force −2mω × v is perpendicular to v and never does work; so the claim that no fictitious force does work is false; and the Euler force −mω̇ × r vanishes when ω is constant.

questions.q: In the northern hemisphere, a ball is rolled due north across a smooth horizontal surface. Ignoring friction, which way does the Coriolis force deflect it?
options: It is not deflected because it moves along a meridian
questions.why: In the northern hemisphere, the horizontal effect of −2mω × v deflects horizontal motion to the right; for a ball heading north that is east. West would be the southern hemisphere result; the vertical component of the Coriolis force for northward motion is zero (it is horizontal for this motion); and northward motion is deflected, since the vertical component of ω is not parallel to v.

questions.q: A bead of mass m slides on a smooth straight wire that rotates in a horizontal plane with constant angular velocity ω about a vertical axis through one end. Working in the rotating frame, find r(t) if the bead starts at rest relative to the wire at r = a, and find the horizontal normal reaction from the wire.
markScheme: Equation along the wire: r̈ = ω²r (centrifugal force mω²r)
Solution with r(0) = a, ṙ(0) = 0: r = a cosh ωt
Coriolis force −2mω × v has magnitude 2mωṙ perpendicular to the wire
Normal reaction balances it: N = 2mωṙ = 2maω² sinh ωt
States direction: in the direction of rotation (the wire pushes the bead forwards)
questions.modelAnswer: In the rotating frame the wire is fixed. Along the wire, the only force is the centrifugal force mω²r (the weight and vertical reaction balance, and the wire is smooth), so r̈ = ω²r. With r(0) = a and ṙ(0) = 0, r = a cosh ωt. Perpendicular to the wire (horizontally), the bead has no acceleration in the rotating frame, so the horizontal normal reaction must cancel the Coriolis force −2mω × v, of magnitude 2mωṙ. Hence N = 2mωṙ = 2maω² sinh ωt, directed in the sense of rotation: the wire pushes the bead round. (Check from the inertial frame: the transverse equation N = m(1/r) d(r²ω)/dt = 2mωṙ.)

questions.q: A rocket in deep space with exhaust speed u relative to the rocket burns fuel until its mass falls from m₀ to m₀/4. By how much does its speed increase?
questions.why: The rocket equation gives Δv = u ln(m₀/m) = u ln 4 ≈ 1.39u. 3u/4 treats the speed gain as proportional to the fraction of mass burnt; 4u uses the mass ratio without the logarithm; and u/4 multiplies u by m/m₀ = 1/4, the final-to-initial mass ratio, again with no logarithm.

questions.q: Two bodies of masses m₁ and m₂ attract each other gravitationally with no external forces. What is the reduced mass in the equation μr̈ = F(r) for r = r₁ − r₂?
questions.why: Subtracting the two equations of motion gives r̈ = F/m₁ + F/m₂ = F(m₁ + m₂)/(m₁m₂), so μ = m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂). The total mass m₁ + m₂ governs the centre of mass and appears in G(m₁ + m₂) in Kepler's third law, but it is not μ; the arithmetic and geometric means have no role here.

questions.q: Derive the equation of motion m dv/dt = −u dm/dt + F for a rocket that ejects mass backwards at speed u relative to itself, and solve it when F = 0.
markScheme: Momentum at t: mv. At t + δt: rocket (m + δm)(v + δv), ejected mass −δm moving at v − u
Sets change in total momentum equal to F δt
Neglects second-order term δm δv to get m δv + u δm = F δt
Divides by δt and takes the limit
With F = 0: dv = −u dm/m, so v − v₀ = u ln(m₀/m)
questions.modelAnswer: At time t the rocket has mass m and velocity v, momentum mv. During δt it ejects mass −δm (δm < 0) with velocity v − u (relative velocity −u). At t + δt the total momentum of rocket plus ejected fuel is (m + δm)(v + δv) + (−δm)(v − u) = mv + m δv + u δm + δm δv. The change in momentum equals the impulse of the external force: m δv + u δm + δm δv = F δt. Dividing by δt and letting δt → 0 (the product term is second order): m dv/dt = −u dm/dt + F. With F = 0, dv = −u dm/m; integrating from (m₀, v₀) to (m, v): v − v₀ = −u ln(m/m₀) = u ln(m₀/m).

questions.q: A solid sphere, a solid cylinder and a hoop, all of the same mass and radius, are released together from rest on the same slope and roll without slipping. In which order do they reach the bottom?
questions.why: The acceleration is g sin α/(1 + I/(Ma²)), with I/(Ma²) = 2/5, 1/2 and 1 for the sphere, cylinder and hoop, so the sphere is fastest and the hoop slowest. The reverse order would hold if more rotational inertia helped, which it does not; they would arrive together only if sliding without friction; and the cylinder has a larger I/(Ma²) than the sphere, so it cannot beat it.

questions.q: What is the moment of inertia of a uniform thin rod of mass M and length L about an axis perpendicular to it through a point L/4 from one end?
questions.why: The point is L/4 from the centre, so the parallel axis theorem gives ML²/12 + M(L/4)² = ML²/12 + ML²/16 = 7ML²/48. ML²/12 is the value about the centre; ML²/3 is about an end; and ML²/16 is only the Md² term without I_cm.

questions.q: A uniform solid sphere of mass M and radius a rolls without slipping down a rough plane inclined at angle α. Find its acceleration and the friction force, and the least coefficient of friction for which rolling without slipping is possible.
markScheme: Along the slope: MA = Mg sin α − F
Torque about centre: (2/5)Ma² ω̇ = Fa
Rolling: A = aω̇
Solves A = (5/7)g sin α and F = (2/7)Mg sin α
Needs F ≤ μN = μMg cos α, so μ ≥ (2/7) tan α
questions.modelAnswer: Let F be the friction up the slope and A the acceleration down it. Newton along the slope: MA = Mg sin α − F. Taking moments about the centre: I ω̇ = Fa with I = (2/5)Ma². Rolling without slipping: A = aω̇. So F = (2/5)MA, and MA = Mg sin α − (2/5)MA, giving A = (5/7)g sin α and F = (2/7)Mg sin α. The normal reaction is N = Mg cos α, and static friction requires F ≤ μN, so (2/7)Mg sin α ≤ μMg cos α, i.e. μ ≥ (2/7) tan α.

questions.q: In frame S, two events occur at the same place, 3 μs apart. In frame S′ they are 5 μs apart. What is the speed of S′ relative to S?
questions.why: The events are at the same place in S, so 3 μs is the proper time and Δt′ = γ × 3 μs = 5 μs gives γ = 5/3, hence β = √(1 − 9/25) = 4/5. 0.6c corresponds to γ = 5/4; 0.75c gives γ = 1/√(1 − 9/16) = 4/√7 ≈ 1.51, not 5/3; and 0.36c is 1 − β² = 1/γ², not β.

questions.q: A spaceship moving at 0.6c relative to Earth fires a probe forward at 0.6c relative to the ship. What is the probe's speed relative to Earth?
questions.why: Relativistic velocity addition gives (0.6 + 0.6)c/(1 + 0.36) = 1.2c/1.36 = 15c/17 ≈ 0.88c. 1.2c is the Galilean sum, which exceeds c; 0.6c ignores the ship's motion; and 0.77c uses the small-velocity approximation 1/(1 + u′v/c²) ≈ 1 − u′v/c², giving 1.2c × 0.64 ≈ 0.77c, which is not valid when u′v/c² = 0.36 is not small.

questions.q: Starting from the Lorentz transformation ct′ = γ(ct − βx), x′ = γ(x − βct), derive the formulae for time dilation and length contraction, stating clearly in which frame each measurement is made.
markScheme: Time dilation: clock at rest in S′ (Δx′ = 0); use inverse transformation cΔt = γ(cΔt′ + βΔx′)
Gives Δt = γΔt′: moving clock runs slow as seen from S
Length: rod at rest in S′, rest length L₀ = Δx′
In S the ends are recorded at the same time (Δt = 0): Δx′ = γ(Δx − βcΔt) = γΔx
So L = Δx = L₀/γ
questions.modelAnswer: Time dilation: a clock at rest in S′ ticks at two events with Δx′ = 0 and Δt′ = Δτ (its proper time). The inverse transformation is ct = γ(ct′ + βx′), so cΔt = γ(cΔt′ + βΔx′) = γcΔt′. Hence Δt = γΔτ > Δτ: observers in S see the moving clock run slow. Length contraction: a rod at rest in S′ along the x′-axis has rest length L₀ = Δx′ (its ends' x′ coordinates, which do not change in time). Observers in S measure its length by recording the positions of both ends at the same S-time, so Δt = 0 and Δx = L. Then Δx′ = γ(Δx − βcΔt) = γL, so L = L₀/γ < L₀.

questions.q: What is the magnitude of the momentum of a particle of mass m with total energy E = 2mc²?
questions.why: E² = p²c² + m²c⁴ gives p²c² = 4m²c⁴ − m²c⁴ = 3m²c⁴, so p = √3 mc. mc divides the kinetic energy E − mc² = mc² by c, which is only right for a massless particle (it would need E = √2 mc²); 2mc confuses E/c with the momentum; and √5 mc adds the squares instead of subtracting.

questions.q: A particle of mass M at rest decays into two photons. What is the energy of each photon?
options: It depends on the direction of emission
questions.why: Momentum conservation makes the photons' momenta equal and opposite, so they have equal energies, and energy conservation shares Mc² between them: Mc²/2 each. Mc² each would double the total energy; Mc²/4 loses half of it; and the direction cannot affect the energies in the rest frame because of the symmetry.

questions.q: Define the 4-momentum P of a particle of mass m moving with velocity u and show that E² = |p|²c² + m²c⁴. Show that for u ≪ c the energy reduces to the rest energy plus the Newtonian kinetic energy.
markScheme: P = mU with U = dX/dτ = γ(u)(c, u), so P = (E/c, p) with E = γmc², p = γmu
P·P = m²U·U = m²c² (U·U = γ²(c² − u²) = c²)
Also P·P = E²/c² − |p|², giving E² = |p|²c² + m²c⁴
Expands γ = (1 − u²/c²)^(−1/2) ≈ 1 + u²/(2c²)
E ≈ mc² + ½mu²
questions.modelAnswer: The 4-velocity is U = dX/dτ, where X = (ct, x) and dτ = dt/γ(u), so U = γ(u)(c, u) and U·U = γ²(c² − |u|²) = c². The 4-momentum is P = mU = (γmc, γmu) = (E/c, p), defining E = γmc² and p = γmu. Then P·P = m²U·U = m²c², and also P·P = E²/c² − |p|². Equating, E² = |p|²c² + m²c⁴. For u ≪ c, γ = (1 − u²/c²)^(−1/2) = 1 + u²/(2c²) + O(u⁴/c⁴), so E = mc² + ½mu² + ..., the rest energy plus the Newtonian kinetic energy, and p ≈ mu.

questions.q:
A particle of mass m moves under the gravitational attraction of a fixed mass M, with force −(GMm/r²) r̂.
(a) Show that the motion is planar and that h = r²θ̇ is constant. Derive the equation d²u/dθ² + u = GM/h², where u = 1/r. [6]
(b) Solve this equation to show that the orbit is a conic r = ℓ/(1 + e cos θ) with the origin at a focus, and express ℓ in terms of h and GM. Show that the energy is E = −(GMm/(2ℓ))(1 − e²). [7]
(c) For an elliptical orbit with semi-major axis a, deduce Kepler's third law T² = 4π²a³/(GM). [4]
(d) A satellite is in a circular orbit of radius R. Its speed is suddenly increased by a factor λ, without change of direction. Find the condition on λ for the satellite to escape. [3]
markScheme: (a) Zero torque, L = mr × ṙ constant, so motion in plane perpendicular to L; h = r²θ̇ constant
(a) u-substitution: ṙ = −h u′, r̈ = −h²u²u″; radial equation gives u″ + u = GM/h²
(b) General solution u = GM/h² + A cos(θ − θ₀); ℓ = h²/(GM), e = Aℓ ≥ 0, choose θ₀ = 0
(b) Energy at perihelion (θ = 0): r = ℓ/(1 + e), ṙ = 0, rθ̇ = h/r, giving E = −(GMm/(2ℓ))(1 − e²)
(c) dA/dt = h/2, area πab, b = a√(1 − e²), ℓ = a(1 − e²), so T = 2πa^(3/2)/√(GM)
(d) Circular speed √(GM/R); escape needs ½mλ²GM/R ≥ GMm/R, so λ ≥ √2
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The force is central, so the torque r × F = 0 and L = m r × ṙ is constant. r is always perpendicular to the fixed vector L, so the motion lies in the plane through O perpendicular to L (if L = 0 the motion is radial, along a line). In plane polars in that plane, |L| = mr²θ̇, so h = r²θ̇ is constant. With u = 1/r, θ̇ = hu², ṙ = −(1/u²)(du/dθ)θ̇ = −h du/dθ and r̈ = −h (d²u/dθ²)θ̇ = −h²u² d²u/dθ². The radial equation m(r̈ − rθ̇²) = −GMmu² becomes −h²u²(u″ + u) = −GMu², so u″ + u = GM/h².

(b) The general solution is u = GM/h² + A cos(θ − θ₀). Choosing axes so that θ₀ = 0 and A ≥ 0, and writing ℓ = h²/(GM) and e = Aℓ, gives 1/r = (1 + e cos θ)/ℓ, i.e. r = ℓ/(1 + e cos θ). This is the polar equation of a conic with eccentricity e and a focus at the origin: an ellipse (e < 1), parabola (e = 1) or hyperbola (e > 1). Energy is constant, so evaluate at θ = 0 where r = ℓ/(1 + e) and ṙ = 0 (dr/dθ = 0 there). Then E = ½m h²/r² − GMm/r = ½m (GMℓ)(1 + e)²/ℓ² − GMm(1 + e)/ℓ = (GMm/ℓ)(1 + e)[(1 + e)/2 − 1] = (GMm/(2ℓ))(1 + e)(e − 1) = −(GMm/(2ℓ))(1 − e²).

(c) For an ellipse, r_min = ℓ/(1 + e) and r_max = ℓ/(1 − e), so 2a = 2ℓ/(1 − e²) and ℓ = a(1 − e²); the semi-minor axis is b = a√(1 − e²). The area swept per unit time is ½r²θ̇ = h/2, so the period is T = πab/(h/2) = 2πab/h. Using h = √(GMℓ) = √(GMa(1 − e²)): T = 2πa · a√(1 − e²)/√(GMa(1 − e²)) = 2πa^(3/2)/√(GM). Hence T² = 4π²a³/(GM).

(d) In a circular orbit GMm/R² = mv²/R, so v = √(GM/R). After the boost the speed is λ√(GM/R) at the same radius, so E = ½mλ²GM/R − GMm/R = (GMm/R)(λ²/2 − 1). The satellite escapes if E ≥ 0, i.e. λ ≥ √2. (λ = √2 gives a parabolic escape orbit; 1 < λ < √2 gives an ellipse with perihelion R.)

questions.q:
(a) Define the proper time along a particle's world line and the 4-momentum P of a particle of mass m. Show that P·P = m²c², and deduce the relation between energy E and momentum p. [5]
(b) A particle of mass M, at rest, decays into two particles of masses m₁ and m₂. Show that the energy of the first is E₁ = (M² + m₁² − m₂²)c²/(2M), and find the magnitude of the momentum of each product. A charged pion of mass 139.6 MeV/c² at rest decays into a muon of mass 105.7 MeV/c² and a neutrino, treated as massless. Find the kinetic energy of the muon to 2 significant figures. [9]
(c) In a fixed-target experiment, a proton of energy E strikes a proton at rest and the reaction p + p → p + p + p + p̄ occurs (p̄ has the proton mass m). Find the minimum kinetic energy of the incoming proton in terms of mc². [6]
markScheme: (a) dτ = dt/γ(u); U = dX/dτ = γ(c, u); P = mU = (E/c, p)
(a) U·U = c², so P·P = m²c² and E² = p²c² + m²c⁴
(b) Conservation P = P₁ + P₂, rearranged to P₂ = P − P₁ and squared
(b) Uses P·P₁ = ME₁ in the rest frame to obtain E₁
(b) |p|c = √((M² − (m₁ + m₂)²)(M² − (m₁ − m₂)²)) c²/(2M), or equivalent via E₁² − m₁²c⁴
(b) Pion: E_μ ≈ 109.8 MeV, kinetic energy ≈ 4.1 MeV
(c) Invariant (P₁ + P₂)² = 2m²c² + 2mE evaluated in lab
(c) Threshold: products at rest in CM frame, (4mc)², giving E = 7mc², kinetic 6mc²
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Along a timelike world line, proper time is the time shown by a clock moving with the particle: dτ = dt/γ(u) = √(c²dt² − |dx|²)/c, a Lorentz invariant. The 4-velocity is U = dX/dτ = γ(u)(c, u) and the 4-momentum is P = mU = (E/c, p) with E = γmc², p = γmu. Since U·U = γ²(c² − |u|²) = c², P·P = m²c². But P·P = E²/c² − |p|², so E² = |p|²c² + m²c⁴.

(b) Conservation of 4-momentum: P = P₁ + P₂ with P = (Mc, 0) in the rest frame. Then P₂ = P − P₁, and squaring: m₂²c² = M²c² + m₁²c² − 2P·P₁. In the rest frame P·P₁ = Mc × E₁/c − 0·p₁ = ME₁. So 2ME₁ = (M² + m₁² − m₂²)c², giving E₁ = (M² + m₁² − m₂²)c²/(2M). The momenta are equal and opposite with magnitude p, where p²c² = E₁² − m₁²c⁴ = c⁴[(M² + m₁² − m₂²)² − 4M²m₁²]/(4M²) = c⁴(M² − (m₁ + m₂)²)(M² − (m₁ − m₂)²)/(4M²). So pc = c²√((M² − (m₁ + m₂)²)(M² − (m₁ − m₂)²))/(2M).
For the pion: E_μ = (139.6² + 105.7²)/(2 × 139.6) MeV = (19488 + 11172)/279.2 MeV ≈ 109.8 MeV. The kinetic energy is E_μ − m_μc² ≈ 109.8 − 105.7 ≈ 4.1 MeV.

(c) Let P₁ = (E/c, p) be the beam proton and P₂ = (mc, 0) the target. The invariant s = (P₁ + P₂)·(P₁ + P₂) = P₁·P₁ + P₂·P₂ + 2P₁·P₂ = m²c² + m²c² + 2(E/c)(mc) = 2m²c² + 2mE. In the centre of momentum frame the total 4-momentum is (E*/c, 0) and the final state has energy at least 4mc² (all four particles at rest in that frame), so s ≥ (4mc)² = 16m²c². Hence 2m²c² + 2mE ≥ 16m²c², giving E ≥ 7mc². The minimum kinetic energy of the incoming proton is E − mc² = 6mc² (about 5.6 GeV for a proton).
